add: **Circular permutation** — arranging the chosen items around a circle instead of leaving them unordered multiplies the count by $(r-1)!$.
**Distribution into cells** — choosing which items go in one cell is a combination; repeating the choice cell by cell is the distribution count.
**Full permutation** — ordering the chosen $r$ items afterwards is what turns $C(n, r)$ into $P(n, r)$.
**Partition into groups** — a partition into two groups is exactly one combination, and the general case is the multinomial extension.
**Permutation with identical items** — a multiset arrangement is a sequence of combinations, one per distinct item type.
**Strong composition** — the number of strong compositions of $n$ into $k$ parts is the single binomial coefficient $\\binom{n-1}{k-1}$.
**Weak composition** — the stars-and-bars argument turns the count into $\\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$, another binomial coefficient.
**Distribution into cells** — assigning each of $n$ distinct items to one of $k$ cells is $k^n$, the same $n^r$ counting read the other way round.
**Pascal's triangle** — the contrast worth seeing: repetition gives powers, while the triangle collects the no-repetition counts.
**Weak composition** — allowing a part to be zero plays the same role here as allowing an option to be reused.
**Pascal's triangle** — the two-group case of a partition is a binomial coefficient, so the triangle is the partition count in miniature.
**Strong composition** — an ordered partition of an integer with every part non-empty, the integer analogue of splitting a set into groups.
**Weak composition** — the same ordered split with empty parts allowed, which is what makes it a stars-and-bars count.
**Partition into groups** — the same multinomial coefficient, read as box sizes rather than as repeat counts.
**Strong composition** — the repeat counts $k_1, \\ldots, k_m$ of a multiset are themselves a composition of $n$ into positive parts.
**Weak composition** — allowing an item type to appear zero times makes the repeat counts a weak composition instead.
**Pascal's triangle** — each row of the triangle sums to $2^n$, while ordering every item instead gives $n!$.
**Permutation with repetition** — reusing items around a circle breaks the rotation argument, because rotations of a repeated pattern can coincide.
